name: Interview statistics, set 4
description: Statistics questions of the kind asked in online assessments and first rounds: standard errors, precision bounds, permutation tests, power, regression to the mean, F tests, leverage, EWMA and GARCH volatility and spurious regression. Each item keeps its own schedule.

items.prose: You have 50 daily returns, taken to be normal. Their sample standard deviation is 1.2%.
items.question: What is the large-sample standard error of that standard deviation, in per cent to 2 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A standard deviation from n normal values has a standard error of about $\sigma/\sqrt{2n}$.

byKey.root-of-n: You divided by the root of 50, the rule for a mean. For a standard deviation, divide by the root of 2n, which is 100.
byKey.divided-by-n: You divided by 50 rather than by a root. The error shrinks with the root of 2n, so divide 1.2 by 10.

explain.text: For normal data the sample standard deviation has a large-sample standard error of $\sigma/\sqrt{2n}$. Here that is $1.2/\sqrt{100} = 0.12$ per cent. A rough 95% range for the true figure is 0.96% to 1.44%.

items.prose: You run 100 independent yes-or-no trials. Each is a success with true chance 0.2.
items.question: What is the smallest standard deviation an unbiased estimator of that chance can have? Give it as a decimal.

feedback.correct: Correct. No unbiased estimator does better than 0.04.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the information in 100 trials and invert it.

byKey.gave-variance: You gave the bound on the variance, 0.0016. The question asks for the standard deviation, which is its root.
byKey.one-trial: You used the information in one trial. With 100 trials the information is 100 times larger, so divide by 100 inside the root.

explain.text: One trial carries information $1/(p(1 - p)) = 6.25$, so 100 trials carry 625. The Cramér-Rao bound on the variance is $1/625 = 0.0016$, a standard deviation of 0.04. The sample proportion reaches the bound.

items.prose: Two desks are watched for 50 days each. Desk A makes a mean of £10.4k a day and desk B £9.6k. Each has a daily standard deviation of £2k. Use 1.96 for a 95% interval.
items.question: What is the lower end of the 95% interval for the gap, in £ thousands to 3 decimal places?

feedback.correct: Correct. The interval starts at 0.016, just above zero.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The gap has the standard errors of both means in it.

byKey.one-mean: You used the error of one mean, $2/\sqrt{50}$. The gap carries both errors, so its error is $\sqrt{0.08 + 0.08} = 0.4$.
byKey.upper-end: You gave the upper end. Subtract 1.96 standard errors from the gap of 0.8 instead.

explain.text: The gap is $10.4 - 9.6 = 0.8$ thousand. Its standard error is $\sqrt{4/50 + 4/50} = 0.4$. The lower end is $0.8 - 1.96 \times 0.4 = 0.016$, just above zero.

items.prose: Your prior on a success rate is uniform from 0 to 1. The first three trials all succeed.
items.question: What is the chance that the fourth trial succeeds? Give it as a decimal or a fraction.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Treat the uniform prior as counts seen before the data.

byKey.no-prior: You used 3/3 and left the prior out. A uniform prior acts like one success and one failure seen before.
byKey.one-failure: You added one failure but no success, giving 3/4. A uniform prior adds one of each, so the chance is 4/5.

explain.text: A uniform prior is Beta(1, 1), so three successes give Beta(4, 1). The chance of a fourth success is its mean, $4/5 = 0.8$. This is Laplace's rule of succession.

items.prose: Group A holds the values 8 and 9, and group B holds 1, 2 and 3. You test whether A has the higher mean by shuffling the five labels.
items.question: What is the one-sided permutation p-value, as a decimal?

feedback.correct: Correct. One split in 10 is as extreme.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the ways to choose which two values form group A.

byKey.ordered-pairs: You counted 20 ordered pairs but only one order of 8 and 9. Count both orders, or use the 10 unordered pairs.
byKey.two-sided: You doubled the p-value for a two-sided test. The question asks only whether A is higher.

explain.text: There are $\binom{5}{2} = 10$ ways to choose which two values form group A. Only 8 and 9 give a gap in means as large as the one seen, 6.5. So the p-value is $1/10 = 0.1$.

items.prose: A test statistic comes out at z = 1.8. You test at the 5% level.
items.question: Is the result significant?

options.text: Yes one-sided, with p = 0.036, but not two-sided, with p = 0.072
Yes both ways, since 1.8 is above the one-sided cut-off of 1.645
options.why: You used the one-sided cut-off for both tests. A two-sided test at 5% needs z beyond 1.96.

options.text: No either way, since a z under 1.96 fails every test at the 5% level
options.why: You used the two-sided cut-off for both tests. A one-sided test at 5% needs only 1.645, and 1.8 clears it.

options.text: Yes two-sided, with p = 0.036, but not one-sided, with p = 0.072
options.why: You swapped the two p-values. The two-sided p-value is double the one-sided one, so it is the larger.

feedback.correct: Correct. Only the one-sided test rejects.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare 1.8 with the one-sided and two-sided 5% cut-offs.

explain.text: The one-sided p-value is $1 - \Phi(1.8) = 0.036$, under 5%. The two-sided p-value doubles it to 0.072, over 5%. Choose the side before you see the data.

items.prose: You backtest two independent strategies with no skill, so each t statistic is standard normal. You keep the strategy with the larger t.
items.question: What is the expected value of the t statistic you keep, to 3 decimal places?

feedback.correct: Correct. Picking the better of two adds about 0.564 with no skill at all.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the larger of two values as their average plus half their gap.

byKey.no-selection: You took the mean of one statistic, 0. Keeping the larger of two picks the better draw, so its mean is above zero.
byKey.one-size: You found the mean size of one statistic, $\sqrt{2/\pi}$. The larger of two exceeds their average by half their gap, which has mean $1/\sqrt{\pi}$.

explain.text: The larger of X and Y is $(X + Y)/2 + |X - Y|/2$. The first part has mean 0, and $X - Y$ has sd $\sqrt{2}$, so $E|X - Y| = 2/\sqrt{\pi}$. The kept t statistic averages $1/\sqrt{\pi} \approx 0.564$.

items.prose: A test needs 150 observations to reach 80% power against the effect you planned for. The true effect turns out to be half that size.
items.question: How many observations give the same power now?

feedback.correct: Correct. Half the effect needs four times the data.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how the test statistic grows with n.

byKey.doubled: You doubled n for half the effect. The test statistic grows with the root of n, so you need four times the data.
byKey.root-two: You scaled n by the root of two. The effect sits beside $\sqrt{n}$, so n must grow by the square of 2.

explain.text: Power depends on the effect times $\sqrt{n}$. Halving the effect needs $\sqrt{n}$ to double, so n grows fourfold. That is $4 \times 150 = 600$ observations.

items.prose: Across funds, the return in one year and the return in the next have correlation 0.5. Each year the mean is 6% and the standard deviation 10%. One fund made 26% this year.
items.question: Using the regression line, what is its expected return next year, in per cent?

feedback.correct: Correct. Half the lead carries over, giving 16%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Forecast the lead over the mean, not the return itself.

byKey.no-pull: You expected the same 26% again. With correlation 0.5, only half of the 20-point lead over the mean carries over.
byKey.halved-return: You halved the whole return. Halve the lead over the mean, 20 points, then add back the mean of 6%.

explain.text: The slope is $0.5 \times 10/10 = 0.5$, so half of the lead over the mean carries over. The lead is $26 - 6 = 20$ points. The forecast is $6 + 0.5 \times 20 = 16$ per cent.

items.prose: A regression with 3 predictors and an intercept is fitted to 44 observations. Its $R^2$ is 0.3.
items.question: What is the overall F statistic, to 2 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide each part of $R^2$ by its degrees of freedom first.

byKey.df-41: You used 41 residual degrees of freedom. Count the intercept too: $44 - 3 - 1 = 40$.
byKey.no-df: You divided $R^2$ by $1 - R^2$ and stopped. Divide each by its degrees of freedom, 3 and 40.

explain.text: F is $(R^2/k)/((1 - R^2)/(n - k - 1))$ with $k = 3$ and $n - k - 1 = 40$. That is $0.1/0.0175 = 5.71$. Each share of $R^2$ is divided by its own degrees of freedom.

items.prose: A straight line is fitted by least squares to five points. Their x values are 1, 2, 3, 4 and 20.
items.question: Which point has the most leverage?

options.text: The point at x = 20, far from the other x values
The point at x = 1, the smallest of the x values
options.why: You picked the smallest x. Leverage grows with distance from the mean x, which is 6, and 1 is only 5 away.

options.text: The point at x = 3, the centre of the first four
options.why: You picked the centre of the cluster. Leverage is measured from the mean of all five x values, which is 6.

options.text: All five have the same leverage in a straight line
options.why: You gave each point the same pull. A point's leverage rises with its squared distance from the mean x.

feedback.correct: Correct. The point at 20 has leverage 0.984.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Leverage depends on how far x is from the mean x.

explain.text: Leverage is $1/n + (x - \bar{x})^2/S_{xx}$, with $\bar{x} = 6$ and $S_{xx} = 250$. At x = 20 it is $0.2 + 196/250 = 0.984$. Every other point has 0.3 or less.

items.prose: A fitted model is $y = 3 + 2x + 4D + 1.5xD$, where D is 1 for one group and 0 for the other.
items.question: What is the fitted value at x = 2 for the group with D = 1?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With D = 1, both the intercept and the slope change.

byKey.no-interaction: You left out the term $1.5xD$, which adds 3 at x = 2 when D = 1.
byKey.other-group: You set D to 0, which gives the other group's fit. With D = 1, add $4 + 1.5 \times 2$ as well.

explain.text: With D = 1 the line is $y = 7 + 3.5x$: the dummy shifts the intercept by 4 and the slope by 1.5. At x = 2 that is $7 + 3.5 \times 2 = 14$.

items.prose: A risk model tracks daily volatility by EWMA with decay 0.94. It went into today at 1%, and then the share moved 3%.
items.question: What is the updated daily volatility, in per cent to 2 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Update the variance, then take the root.

byKey.averaged-vols: You averaged the volatilities, $0.94 \times 1 + 0.06 \times 3$. EWMA averages variances, so square first and take the root last.
byKey.weights-swapped: You put 0.94 on today's squared return. The decay 0.94 weights yesterday's variance, and the new return gets 0.06.

explain.text: EWMA updates the variance: $0.94 \times 1^2 + 0.06 \times 3^2 = 1.48$. The new volatility is $\sqrt{1.48} \approx 1.22$ per cent. A single 3% day lifts the estimate by more than a fifth.

items.prose: A GARCH(1,1) model of daily returns has $\omega = 0.0000045$, $\alpha = 0.10$ and $\beta = 0.88$.
items.question: What is the long-run daily volatility, in per cent to 1 decimal place?

feedback.correct: Correct. The long-run volatility is 1.5% a day.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the long-run variance first, then take its root.

byKey.annualised: You scaled the figure to a year. The question asks for the daily volatility, the root of 0.000225.
byKey.one-minus-beta: You divided $\omega$ by $1 - \beta$ alone. The long-run variance divides by $1 - \alpha - \beta = 0.02$.

explain.text: The long-run variance is $\omega/(1 - \alpha - \beta) = 0.0000045/0.02 = 0.000225$. Its root is 0.015, or 1.5% a day. The closer $\alpha + \beta$ is to 1, the slower the pull back to this level.

items.prose: You simulate two random walks that are independent of each other. You regress the level of one on the level of the other by least squares.
items.question: What should you expect from the usual t statistic of the slope?

options.text: It lands beyond 1.96 in size far more often than 5% of the time
It stays near zero, as it does for two unrelated series of data
options.why: You treated the levels as independent draws. Each walk drifts, so the two often trend together by chance.

options.text: It can be trusted whenever the fitted $R^2$ of the regression is high
options.why: You took a high $R^2$ as proof. Regressions of one walk on another often show a high $R^2$ too.

options.text: It becomes a valid test once the walks run for more than 100 steps
options.why: You expected more data to fix it. With walks, a longer sample makes false rejections more common, not less.

feedback.correct: Correct. The usual t test rejects far too often for two walks.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the levels of a random walk are independent draws.

explain.text: Random walks wander, so least squares finds slopes that the usual errors call significant. In 1,000 simulated pairs of 500 steps, 88.0% had a t statistic beyond 1.96 in size. After differencing both series, 5.0% did, close to the 5% of a valid test.
